newsitem.title: GERMANY: FDP tax cut demands strain German coalition.
newsitem.headline: FDP tax cut demands strain German coalition.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), increasingly a loose cannon in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling alliance, strained coalition ties on Monday by demanding the abolition by 2000 of a tax levied to rebuild eastern Germany.

At their traditional conference at Epiphany -- when the three kings brought gifts for the infant Jesus -- FDP chiefs said they hoped tax giveaways would win them enough votes to survive as a national political force at general elections next year.

Party leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told delegates in the southern city of Stuttgart that scrapping the so-called solidarity surcharge "has become a symbol of whether the state will cut the tax burden on citizens and businesses".

Opinion polls say the FDP is dangerously close to the minimum five percent of votes required to guarantee reelection to parliament. Under the threat, it has turned into a tax-cutting single-issue party.

But calls for the solidarity surcharge's abolition have angered the powerful Christian Democrats (CDU) in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition. The demand comes soon after a previous row was settled by agreeing a two-point cut in the tax to 5.5 percent in 1998.

"Discussing the solidarity tax has become the FDP's hobby," Michael Glos, parliamentary chief of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), told German radio. The CSU is the CDU's sister party in Bavaria.
Glos added that the FDP wanted to deny support to eastern Germany, a region which still needed resources to rebuild its economy more than six years after unification with the rich west.

State transfers to the east have run at a huge 150 billion marks ($95 billion) a year since 1990 but have failed to make a dent in unemployment there, which is stuck at 15 percent -- a figure which has been kept down through costly job creation schemes.
Kohl's CDU has already repudiated the FDP tax demands. Powerful parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble said Germany could not afford the cut.
"Anyone who claims the opposite has no right to be taken seriously," Schaeuble said last week.
Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said the row was turning the solidarity tax into a political football being kicked around in Bonn.

"A decision on when and how the solidarity tax should be reduced should be linked to concrete progress in rebuilding east Germany," Manfred Stolpe, SPD premier of the eastern state of Brandenburg, told Monday's Handelsblatt newspaper.

The renewed tax row comes just as a coalition working group is finalising a major tax reform project intended to bring big income tax cuts in 1999 while guaranteeing Germany can stick to the borrowing limits required under European monetary union.
The commission's work is already behind schedule. The reopening of the coalition's war of words could mean it might miss its target to finalise its tax strategy this month.
FDP leaders also called for reform of education and pensions, cuts in state spending -- now over 50 percent of gross domestic product -- and changes to Germany's pay bargaining system.

But the FDP still regards tax cutting as its top priority. Talking to Monday's mass-circulation Bild newspaper, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, also a member of the FDP, linked the solidarity tax issue to the whole tax reform debate.
"There is no point trying to stimulate the economy with a major tax reform while retaining the solidarity tax," Rexrodt said. "The solidarity tax must go by the year 2000." ($1=1.5653 Mark)
